# Iceland Highlands 2023

## Overview

Four days in the highlands in August 2023, in a grey Dacia Duster rented from the city depot and returned with a cracked mud flap and a boot full of volcanic dust. The Duster is the smallest vehicle that will take the F-roads without drama, and it handled the washboard and the gravel better than I expected. I drove with one other person, shared the fuel and the driving, and slept in huts and a tent. The weather ran from bright and cold to a horizontal drizzle that lasted an afternoon. I booked nothing beyond the first hut and relied on the road conditions being kind, which they were. The highlands are empty in a way the coast is not, and whole hours passed without another vehicle. Fuel stops are far apart, so I carried a full jerry can as a matter of course and never once regretted the space it took. I took a spare wheel and a pump and checked the tyres at every stop, because a flat on the gravel would have cost the day. The midges were bad near the huts in the evening, and I used a head net more than once. I met almost no one on the interior tracks, and the solitude was the point as much as the landscape. The colours of the rhyolite and the obsidian are the memory I keep, and the hot river at the hut was the reward at the end of each walking day.

## Route

I started from the south and climbed toward Landmannalaugar on the F208, a road of loose gravel and slow bends that took two hours to cover the ground a normal road would eat in forty minutes. The last stretch crosses a river, and I walked it first to read the depth and the line of stones before driving through in low gear. The crossing was shallow that day, well under the wheel hubs, but it was the part of the trip I had thought about most.

At Landmannalaugar I stayed two nights in the mountain hut, a long timber building with bunks, a kitchen and a hot spring a short walk across the lava field. The spring is the reward at the end of a walking day: warm water, cold air, steam rising off the surface. From the hut I walked the marked trails each morning, one up the yellow rhyolite slopes and one along the obsidian field. The colours there are not like anything on the coast, ochre and green and near-black under a low sun.

From Landmannalaugar I took the F208 north and west, past a second crossing and a stretch of black sand, then joined the main track that opens onto the interior plain. Fuel came from a jerry can at the halfway point, poured in with a funnel while the wind tried to take the funnel away. The total distance for the four days came to about 1200 km, most of it on gravel at low speed, and the Duster drank more than its road figure the whole way. The marked trails are well signed, and I never needed a guide, only a good map and the willingness to turn back when the weather moved in. I crossed the river twice more without trouble, reading each from the bank before driving.

## Costs

The rental was the biggest single line at 620 EUR for four days including the gravel insurance, which I would not skip on these roads. Fuel came to about 260 EUR for the 1200 km, high because the gravel and the low gears wreck the economy. The hut at Landmannalaugar cost 65 EUR a night for a bunk, and the campsite the other night was 20 EUR. Food I carried in, about 90 EUR of groceries from the city before I left, and I ate one meal out near the end for 35 EUR.

The river crossings cost nothing but the care I gave them, and the hot spring was included with the hut. Total spend landed near 1400 EUR for the four days, split two ways, which put the trip within reach of a long weekend. I would budget the same again and add a day at the hut if the weather allowed. The ferry I took to the mainland island was a small extra I had not counted, about 20 EUR, and the campsite at the coast the last night was 18 EUR. I would add a little for the bridge toll and the odd coffee stop, and I would set the budget nearer 1500 EUR next time.
